name: wcp
workload: Copying 20 files of 512MiB, 7,000 files of 1MiB and 200,000 files of 1KiB on NVMe
hardware: 64GB RAM, Samsung NVMe SSD (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Experimental tool, Linux only (io_uring); not a full cp replacement.
caveats: Compiler and flags not stated; CPU not stated; last commit 2021; first-party numbers; README text for the figures read via page summary.

name: fcp
workload: Copy Linux kernel source tree and a directory of 13x512MB files, on AWS a1.metal XFS SSD and macOS APFS
claimed_speedup: Linux kernel tree: ~675ms vs cp ~6.02s (about 10x); 13x512MB: ~8s vs ~11.3s (1.4x); macOS kernel tree about 6x, large files 822x (copy-on-write)
hardware: AWS a1.metal (16 CPUs, 32 GiB, SSD, XFS); 2018 MacBook Pro i9 APFS
tradeoffs: Only common cp use cases; tuned for SSD, may be slow on HDD; Unix only.
caveats: Results shown as images; benchmark scripts and compiler flags not checked; the 822x macOS figure comes from APFS copy-on-write clones, not data copying. Rust, not C/C++-callable.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'fast file copy tool faster than cp'

name: diskus
workload: Total size of a 15GB folder (100k directories, 400k files), hyperfine, cold and warm cache
claimed_speedup: Cold cache 1.746s vs du -sh 17.776s (10.18x); warm cache 500.3ms vs 1098.3ms (2.20x)
tradeoffs: Total size only, no per-directory breakdown; Rust.
caveats: Hyperfine commands shown but compiler flags and CPU model absent; first-party.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'fast disk usage tool du alternative'

name: gdu
workload: Scan a 90GB directory with hyperfine, cold and warm cache
claimed_speedup: Cold cache gdu -npc 4.716s vs du -hs 30.608s and ncdu 33.163s; warm cache 466.1ms vs du 1255.2ms and ncdu 2222.4ms
tradeoffs: Optimised for SSD; diskus is faster in the same table; Go binary.
caveats: Hardware and CPU not read; first-party table; gdu loses to diskus on warm cache.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'fast disk usage tool du alternative'

name: rawscan
workload: Read an 11.2GB file of 55.6M lines already in RAM, matching a hex prefix per line
claimed_speedup: User CPU: rawscan 1.60s vs fgets 2.61s vs getline 2.36s vs grep 4.38s (30-40% less CPU than fgets/getline)
hardware: Ryzen 1700, plenty of RAM, average of 10 runs
tradeoffs: Zero-copy pointers into an internal buffer; relies on rawmemchr and sentinel page; Linux/glibc oriented.
caveats: License file exists (LICENSE.md) but SPDX id not confirmed, so usability is reference; compiler flags not read; the author notes Rust bstr is faster; CPU time not wall time.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'fast line reader library faster than fgets getline'

name: rust-linereader
workload: Read a 976MB, 10.3M line file on a Westmere Xeon 2.1GHz, FreeBSD/ZFS
claimed_speedup: next_batch 0.27s (38.3M lines/s) vs read_until 1.94s (5.3M lines/s), read_line 2.54s, lines() 3.23s
tradeoffs: Line length limited by buffer size; author says bstr for_byte_line performs similarly without that limit.
caveats: Baseline is the Rust standard library, not POSIX read; abandoned since 2019; flags not stated; superseded by bstr by author's own note.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'fast line reader library faster than getline'
